mcqs.question: A server holds a user's shopping cart in local memory, so the team adds sticky sessions to make it work without touching application code. What does this convenience actually paper over?
options: A missing caching layer that should sit in front of the database
A bug in the load balancer's routing algorithm
A stateful design where session data lives only on one server instead of somewhere every server can reach
An unnecessary use of cookies that could be replaced with query parameters
mcqs.explanation: Sticky sessions are a workaround for exactly one root cause: state living in one server's local memory instead of a shared store. There's no caching-layer gap or routing bug implied, and cookies vs query parameters is unrelated to the actual problem being papered over.

mcqs.question: A service with sticky sessions adds two new servers to handle a traffic spike. What happens to the load on existing pinned clients' original servers?
options: It drops immediately, since new capacity is always shared across all existing sessions
It drops gradually over the next few minutes as the load balancer rebalances pinned clients
It disappears because sticky sessions expire automatically the moment new servers are added
It stays exactly the same, since existing pinned clients remain committed to their original server and only new sessions can land on the new servers
mcqs.explanation: This is the scaling-friction cost directly — pinned clients are already committed to their original node, so adding capacity does nothing for them; it only helps brand-new sessions. There's no automatic rebalancing or expiration mechanism that would move already-pinned clients.

mcqs.question: A product requires that an admin be able to instantly revoke a specific user's session (for example, after a password reset). Which session-state approach makes this straightforward?
options: An external session store like Redis, where revoking is just deleting that session's key
A JWT-based approach, where the token remains valid until it naturally expires unless a blocklist is added
Sticky sessions alone, since pinning already limits which server holds the session
DNS-based session state, since DNS records can be updated to invalidate a session
mcqs.explanation: Instant revocation is exactly the external store's strength — delete the key and the session is gone everywhere immediately. Plain JWTs stay valid until expiry unless you bolt on an extra blocklist, undercutting 'straightforward.' Sticky sessions don't manage revocation at all, and DNS has nothing to do with per-user session state.

mcqs.question: A service relies purely on sticky sessions (no external session store) to keep users logged in. A rolling deploy cycles every server one at a time. What is the likely visible effect on users?
options: No visible effect, since sticky sessions are designed to survive deploys automatically
A spike of users getting logged out or losing cart contents, concentrated during the deploy window as each pinned server is cycled
Users are automatically migrated to the new server with their session intact, with zero data loss
The load balancer pauses all traffic during the deploy, so no user is ever affected
mcqs.explanation: Stickiness alone doesn't survive the pinned server disappearing — there's no automatic migration or built-in deploy-safety mechanism, and load balancers don't pause all traffic for a rolling deploy. The realistic outcome is a visible cluster of broken sessions concentrated exactly during the deploy, which is this pitfall's core lesson.

mcqs.question: Why can't a WebSocket connection simply be made stateless the way an HTTP session can be moved to an external store?
options: WebSockets don't support any form of shared state at all
The connection itself is a long-lived, pinned link between one client and one server process — there's no per-request routing to make stateless, since there's no new request being made
WebSockets are actually stateless already and need no special handling
Moving WebSocket state to Redis is standard practice and eliminates the pinning entirely
mcqs.explanation: A WebSocket's pinning happens at the transport layer (one open TCP connection), not the application layer, so there's no request to reroute — the fix is sharing data across servers via a bus like Redis pub/sub while the connection itself stays pinned, not eliminating the pinning. WebSockets do support sharing application state; they just can't avoid the connection-level pinning itself.

mcqs.question: How does routing by a consistent hash of a request key improve on cookie-based sticky sessions when a server fails?
options: It behaves identically to sticky sessions in every respect
It eliminates cache locality entirely in exchange for safety
Only the slice of keys hashed to the failed server needs to move, rather than every client pinned by a cookie all failing at once
It requires every request to hit an external session store, removing any locality benefit
mcqs.explanation: Consistent hashing's whole point is that losing one node only remaps that node's slice of the key space, unlike cookie-based stickiness where every client pinned to the dead server loses their session simultaneously. It still preserves most of the cache-locality benefit stickiness aims for, rather than discarding it or requiring an external store per request.
